displayQuote: When a subject becomes totally obsolete we make it a required course

meta.title: Who really said "When a subject becomes totally obsolete we make it a required course"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Peter Drucker really is behind it — but he printed a different sentence in 1969. The familiar one-liner is documented from a 1976 biography's appendix.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When a subject becomes totally obsolete we make it a required course'?
meta.ogDescription: Drucker's own 1969 wording was different, and he changed it again in 1992. The crisp one-liner is documented from 1976. Here is the whole citation trail.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The joke is genuinely Drucker’s — he put it in print himself in The Age of Discontinuity (Harper & Row, 1969, page 193), but in different words: “If a subject has become obsolete, the university faculty makes a required course out of it.” The crisp one-liner people quote is not in that book; its earliest documented appearance is a 1976 appendix of Drucker remarks assembled by his biographer John J. Tarrant, per Quote Investigator ↗.

source.heading: The documented record

docMeta.dd: The Age of Discontinuity: Guidelines to Our Changing Society
Harper & Row, New York, 1969 — quote page 193 (verified on paper by Quote Investigator)
John J. Tarrant, Drucker: The Man Who Invented the Corporate Society, Cahners Books, Boston, 1976 — appendix, page 260

source.excerpt: Organization is always in danger of being overwhelmed by yesterday’s tasks and being rendered sterile by them. If a subject has become obsolete, the university faculty makes a required course out of it—and this “solves the problem” for the time being.
trail: 1969 — Drucker puts the idea in print himself, in The Age of Discontinuity (Harper & Row): “If a subject has become obsolete, the university faculty makes a required course out of it.” Quote Investigator verified the passage on paper at page 193 ↗.

1976 — The compact one-liner surfaces in John J. Tarrant’s biography Drucker: The Man Who Invented the Corporate Society, in what QI calls “a ten-page appendix filled with remarks by Peter Drucker,” at page 260; the Fall 1976 Wharton Magazine reprinted sayings from that appendix. Both citations are logged by Quote Investigator ↗.

1977–1988 — The one-liner is carried forward by quotation anthologies, each crediting Drucker: Peter’s Quotations (1977, page 117), The Book of Quotes (1979, page 170) and The Dictionary of Outrageous Quotations (1988, page 29). All three verified on paper ↗.

1992 — Drucker returns to the joke in Managing for the Future, calling it a university motto: “when a subject becomes totally obsolete, then a required course should be built around it.” Quote Investigator, page 339 ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is Drucker’s own printed sentence, not the one-liner. Note what the compression drops: the 1969 version names the university faculty as the actor and adds the sting about pretending the problem is solved. The familiar “we make it a required course” is the 1976 compilation form.

author.name: Peter Drucker
author.heading: Who was Peter Drucker?
author.metaLine: 1909–2005 · Austrian-American management consultant, educator and author
author.bio: Peter Ferdinand Drucker was born in Vienna in 1909 and died in California in 2005, eight days short of his ninety-sixth birthday. Wikipedia describes him ↗ as an Austrian American management consultant, educator and author “whose writings contributed to the philosophical and practical foundations of modern management theory.” He taught at Sarah Lawrence, Bennington, NYU and Claremont Graduate University, and wrote books — The Practice of Management, The Effective Executive, The Age of Discontinuity — that turned management into a subject you could actually study. He was also a reliable wit about institutions that refuse to change, which is exactly the vein this line comes from.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The name on this quote is right. What travels wrongly is the sentence — the version everyone repeats is a compressed form that Drucker never printed in either of the two books where he made the joke himself.

items.who: Peter Drucker — but not as he wrote it
items.why: Quote sites present “When a subject becomes totally obsolete we make it a required course” as though it were lifted from a Drucker book. It was not. His 1969 sentence runs “If a subject has become obsolete, the university faculty makes a required course out of it,” and his 1992 sentence casts it as a university motto, per Quote Investigator’s paper-verified citations ↗.

items.scope: Where the popular wording actually comes from
items.why: Tarrant’s Drucker: The Man Who Invented the Corporate Society closes with what Quote Investigator describes as “a ten-page appendix filled with remarks by Peter Drucker,” and the familiar one-liner sits there at page 260 — a compiler’s rendering of Drucker’s remarks, not a passage from one of his own books. See the citation ↗.

Once the compact form existed it was copied wholesale: Peter’s Quotations (1977), Barbara Rowes’ The Book of Quotes (1979) and The Dictionary of Outrageous Quotations (1988) all carry it credited to Drucker, each verified on paper by Quote Investigator ↗. Anthology-to-anthology copying is why the 1976 phrasing, not Drucker’s, became the standard text.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit Drucker with the thought — Quote Investigator concludes he can properly be credited with the saying ↗ — but if you want his actual sentence, quote the 1969 one.

context.heading: Why a management writer was picking on universities
lead: Drucker was not making a cheap crack about professors. The 1969 sentence sits inside an argument about organizational inertia — his claim that every institution, however clever, drifts toward protecting what it already does. Yesterday’s task has a department, a budget and a defender; tomorrow’s has nobody. A required course, in that reading, is what an institution builds when it wants to look like it has settled a question instead of actually settling it.

He kept returning to the joke because he kept making the same point. By 1992, in Managing for the Future, he had reframed it as a standing “motto” of American universities, sitting right after the line that there is nothing more reactionary than a liberal faculty — the setup for an argument that universities, like businesses, have to learn how to innovate or stop being useful.
context.detailsSummary: The three versions, side by side
detailsBody: 1969, in Drucker’s own book: “If a subject has become obsolete, the university faculty makes a required course out of it” — and this “solves the problem” for the time being.
1976, in Tarrant’s appendix of Drucker remarks: “When a subject becomes totally obsolete we make it a required course.” This is the version the internet quotes.
1992, in Drucker’s own book again: “It is the motto of the U.S. universities that when a subject becomes totally obsolete, then a required course should be built around it.”

Quote Investigator declines to crown one of these the “real” quotation, concluding instead that Drucker can properly be credited with the saying and that a reader may pick whichever of the three versions suits.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this exact saying and concluded Drucker can properly be credited with it, documenting versions from 1969 (The Age of Discontinuity, Harper & Row, p. 193), 1976 (Tarrant, Drucker: The Man Who Invented the Corporate Society, Cahners Books, appendix p. 260, plus The Wharton Magazine Fall 1976 p. 14), 1977 Peter's Quotations p. 117, 1979 The Book of Quotes p. 170, 1988 The Dictionary of Outrageous Quotations p. 29, and 1992 Managing for the Future, Truman Talley Books/Dutton, p. 339 — most marked 'Verified on paper'. QI also describes Tarrant's appendix as 'a ten-page appendix filled with remarks by Peter Drucker' and reproduces the 1969 and 1992 passages.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of Peter F. Drucker, The age of discontinuity; guidelines to our changing society, Harper & Row, New York, 1969, 428 pages.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of John J. Tarrant, Drucker, the man who invented the corporate society, Cahners Books, 1976, 330 pages.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of Peter F. Drucker, Managing for the future: the 1990s and beyond, Truman Talley Books/Dutton, New York, 1992.

Wikipedia states Peter Ferdinand Drucker (19 November 1909 – 11 November 2005) was an Austrian American management consultant, educator, and author 'whose writings contributed to the philosophical and practical foundations of modern management theory', and lists The Age of Discontinuity (1969) and Managing for the Future (1992) among his books.

Wikiquote's Peter Drucker page does not contain this quote anywhere — neither 'required course' nor 'obsolete' appears on it — and its only Misattributed entry is 'Culture eats strategy for breakfast.'

The Drucker Institute's biography page gives Drucker's dates as November 19, 1909 – November 11, 2005 (dying eight days before his ninety-sixth birthday), notes his teaching at Sarah Lawrence, Bennington, NYU and Claremont Graduate University, and lists his major books including The Age of Discontinuity.
